title: Operations, security and recovery
summary: Detect failures, prove backups can restore and assign incident decisions.
why: A backup needs a tested recovery process.
Least privilege and separate environments limit the impact of mistakes and exposure.
know: RTO is the acceptable recovery time; RPO is the acceptable data-loss window. Set both from business needs.
Use secure connections for accounts and secrets. Review and revoke staff, vendor and agent access.
Monitor availability, critical tasks, errors and backups. Check update compatibility and retain a recovery path.
inputs: Systems, permissions, backup locations and recovery requirements
Incident owners, contacts, change windows and contractual responsibilities
actions: Check least privilege, retention and update procedures; record fixable risks.
Restore in isolation and measure recovery time and missing data.
Set monitoring thresholds, recipients and escalation owners. Test actual alert delivery.
Stabilize service and preserve evidence during incidents. Record the timeline, impact, repair and follow-up.
done: Actual restore results exist; alerts reach the right on-call role.
Incidents and changes have versions, owners and traceable records without exposed secrets.
pitfalls: Promising uncontracted 24/7 support or response SLAs.
Deleting incident records or restoring old data without reconciliation.
decision: Agree on incident authority, communication and acceptable downtime and data loss.

reader.concept: Operations keeps services available. Incident preparation gives the team a way to detect, handle and recover from failures.
reader.when: Use this for hosting handoff, backups or recovery that currently depends on one person.

example.situation: Daily backups exist, but a failure reveals they cannot restore the data.
example.lesson: Practice restoration before relying on a backup.

reader.first_step: Decide acceptable downtime and data loss, then inspect the backups.
terms: The acceptable time to restore service.
